subject: cardboardRobot
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: kid in a cardboard-box robot costume.
Style: cardboard craft.
reasoning:
I'm designing a kid-sized cardboard robot costume: a box torso with painted buttons and foil details, a box helmet with cutout eye holes revealing the kid's face, and foil-wrapped hose tubing for the arms.

Now I'm figuring out the craft materials and texture — corrugated cardboard, kraft tape, marker-drawn dials, foil, bottle-cap antennas, googly eyes — then working out the skeleton proportions for a roughly 1.15m tall six or seven-year-old in a T-pose, placing joints like hips, spine, chest, neck, head, and limb segments at specific heights.

I'm sketching the box helmet as five cardboard panels with a cut-out window so the kid's face stays visible, sizing it around 0.34 wide by 0.3 tall by 0.32 deep with a 0.2 by 0.17 window, and planning the torso as an open-top/bottom box roughly 0.42 wide by 0.46 tall by 0.3 deep to sit over the child's body like a robot suit.

Total height with antenna lands around 1.45m, with the torso box spanning roughly 0.50-0.97. I'm sketching concrete numbers now: floor at y=0, red sneakers with 0.2 foot length, ankle at 0.065, and deciding whether legs are cardboard tubes wrapped in foil or just the kid's own legs in grey sweatpants.

I'll go with the kid's legs in blue jeans, hip at y=0.45, knee at 0.25, ankle at 0.065, plus small cardboard shin-guard boxes (about 0.14×0.18×0.15) with foil cap bands over the lower legs. I'm adjusting the torso box bottom to sit around 0.50-0.52 so a bit of jeans peeks out below it near the pelvis, with thighs about 0.2 long down to the knee and shins roughly 0.19 down to the ankle.

Setting up the leg joint chains...

I'll shorten the leg chain to end at the ankle with three named joints, then add a separate toe joint parented to the leg tip, aimed along the foot direction. Shoes attach to the ankle bone, and now I'm thinking through arm placement for a T-pose-like stance with limbs extended outward.

For the arm costume, I'm picturing foil duct-tube sleeves for the upper arms, red-tape forearm sleeves, and skin-toned hands with simplified finger chains—balancing joint budget by keeping each finger to two joints plus a thumb, roughly twenty joints per hand.

I'll leave a small gap at the elbow between tubes for the kid's visible arm with a rubber band, then build the arm tubes as rods with ngon cross-sections and flat caps, using a crinkled foil-style paint with noise-based facets for the metallic look.

For the head, I'm placing the kid's skull as a small scaled sphere at the neck joint, with a separate jaw piece for the chin and mouth boundary, and layering in face decals for eyes, eyebrows, nose, blush, and freckles, plus messy brown hair peeking through the helmet's visor window.

I'll add a thin pink lip line decal where the jaw meets the head to hide the seam, with a smiley mouth decal (white teeth, dark interior) covering the join. For face layout, I'm placing the head center at (0,1.1,0.01), eyes at y=1.12 with round kid-style textures (white, brown iris, highlight), and working out the helmet's face window depth relative to the head position.

Now I'm sizing the helmet itself: roughly 0.36w × 0.32h × 0.34d centered at (0,1.12,0), with the front panel at z=0.17 and the face window spanning y=1.03–1.2, nudging the head slightly forward so the face sits at z=0.12. I'm also checking the neck and torso proportions so the helmet bottom overlaps cleanly with the torso top, and deciding to skip the folded flaps on top since the helmet would cover them anyway.

I'm reconsidering spacing so a small neck gap peeks between the helmet and torso — raising the helmet bottom to y=1.0, torso top to 0.97, head center at 1.11 — but when I check the chin position against the helmet's bottom edge, it ends up sitting too low, below the opening.

Adjusting the front window placement to run from 1.045 to 1.235 keeps the chin visible properly, and with the helmet top at 1.32 and antennas reaching about 1.48, the overall costume proportions work out cute even if a bit oversized for the kid's frame. Now I'm setting up the torso as a simple kraft-colored box geometry for the body construction.

For front details, I'm adding a control panel rectangle, cylindrical dials, bottle-cap buttons with ridged edges, a hand-drawn gauge, glowing red and green LED bits, a heart emblem, vent slats made of thin dark boxes, a power lever, and a "ROBO-KID" label on the back, plus dark ring decals at the arm holes where the tubes poke through.

For the cardboard itself, I'm painting a kraft-colored base with subtle corrugation ripple lines along one axis, darker exposed edges where flaps would be cut, blended with noise-based tan variation and faint grime near the bottom, computed per-world-position so it stays crisp on the box geometry. Then I'm compositing all the front torso details—panel, dials, gauge, buttons, vents, heart, label, tape strips—into one large SVG decal applied as a textured plane slightly offset in front of the torso.

Beyond that I'm planning out a fuller texture list: torso front and back panels (with lettering and battery drawing), helmet front frame and a side panel with speaker grille circles and bolts, separate eye and mouth decals, extra face details like brows and freckles, a sneaker star decal, and a torn-edge tape texture, alongside separate 3D pieces for caps, dials, levers, and lights.

I'm also sketching smaller accent pieces like a "FRAGILE" sticker for a shin box, hair tuft cards, and a star sticker for the helmet top. For hair, I'm thinking of a scalp cap mesh with tuft cards layered as bangs peeking through the helmet window near the forehead, while the helmet top itself covers most of the head. For antennas, I'm considering using a coil shape from a clockwork kit import, though that dependency might be risky if it's not available.

Rather than relying on external kit imports for the coil and glow effects, I decide to implement both myself — a hand-written helical catmull curve for the coil and a simple local glow function that clones and brightens emissive materials, since that avoids any import path uncertainty. For the antenna tips, I'm planning one ending in a small glowing bead like a light bulb and the other topped with a star shape.

Now I'm sketching out the helmet's finer details: cardboard-tube-stub ears on the sides with foil-covered ends, a bottle-cap light and vent slats on top, and a front panel with a window frame, marker-drawn lightning bolts, and maybe a "ROBOT" label strip instead of trying to draw eyebrows or a face.

I'm adding craft texture to the top — a taped seam, lifted flaps suggesting a hinged lid, and silver duct tape strips across the box corners. For the kid's hands, I'm keeping them bare-skinned with a simple pose, arms out and palms down with fingers spread.

Now I'm planning the finger joint chains (base, mid, tip per digit) and working out the arm direction and roll for the left arm, then importing the builder helper functions I'll need for geometry construction — frames, lines, aiming, offsets, interpolation, and shading utilities from the SDK.

I'm also sketching out a flat color palette, limiting it to a small set of named hex values for materials like kraft paper, tape, duct tape silver, and basic marker/skin tones, while keeping shading paints separate from the raw palette count.

Writing cardboard texture paint...

I'll add subtle counter-shading, mixing lighter tones where the normal faces upward. For texel density, I'm checking that a 1024px paint sheet gives roughly 3mm per texel across the ~6m² painted area, which is plenty fine to resolve the 0.014 ridge pattern.

Actually I want sharper detail, so I'll bump the paint sheet to 2048px. For the foil material, I'm defining a crinkled surface using Voronoi cells to create faceted panels, blending base gray tones with noise variation and darkening the cell edges for a crumpled foil look -- this could work well for duct-like tubes on the arms. Now I'm setting up the builder with the 2048 paint size and starting to define the skeleton, beginning with the hip joint placement.

Working through the spine chain next, I'm using a catmull-rom curve through four points to create spine1, spine2, and chest joints parented to the hips, making sure the span count matches the name count correctly. Then I'm figuring out the neck and head placement -- deciding whether to use a short two-joint chain or simplify to single joints, positioning the neck above the chest and the head further up with a slight forward aim.

Now I'm defining the jaw joint, positioning its hinge near the ear and aiming it forward toward the chin so rotation about the hinge axis swings the jaw down naturally, then moving into the shoulder and arm setup with a chain running outward from the chest through the shoulder and down the arm.

Defining palm geometry...

To avoid that ambiguity I'll use parts for the palm and build fingers with sweep-based chains along paths instead, since those are orientation-free for circular cross-sections, spreading them in Z with the palm facing down.

Still defining joint chains...

I'll set up a generic hand function that mirrors coordinates by side while keeping the thumb pointing forward for both hands, with tapered finger radii and hexagonal cross-sections. Then I'm defining leg chains with hip, knee, and ankle joints, mirrored similarly by side.

For the jeans, I'm sweeping tapered rings along each leg chain with keyed radii, and thinking about adding cuffed hems at the ankles plus deciding whether to give the kid shorts or scuffed-knee jeans to match the costume.

For texture, I'm applying a denim grain pattern with knee patches as lighter decals. Then for the boots, I'm sizing a shin box around the lower leg geometry, positioning it between knee and ankle, and rigging it to the knee joint so it moves naturally with the leg.

Now I'm figuring out the shoes: a white sole box sized and positioned beneath the ankle to complete the sneaker look.

Working out sneaker geometry split into heel sole and toe sole boxes, positioning the toe joint around z=0.07 so the ankle and toe segments align properly...

Still writing sneaker shapes... then I'll start detailing the torso box dimensions and front panel placement for the texture plane.

Planning the panel layout with a round gauge dial, bar graph, colored button row, vent grille lines, a heart-shaped "ROBO" label, diagonal tape strip corners, and a handwritten "MAX 7 YRS" tag, arranged within a 200x196 canvas starting with a white paper rectangle for the top panel.

Still writing SVG elements...

So viewer's right confirms +X direction, matching the model's left side on the viewer's right as expected. I'm defining the torso front plane mapping coordinates to world space, then setting up parameters for placing knobs and cylinder components on that surface.

For bottle caps I'm sketching a simple approach — a short outer cylinder plus a thinner inner disc for the top, maybe with multiple sides for a crimped look. Then I'm planning the wiring: a curvy colored sweep connecting a panel to a plug fitting.

Now I'm working out the arm holes — dark flat cylinders at the shoulder positions ringed with tan tape, sized slightly larger than the arm tubes so the tubes can pass through and emerge visibly from the torso box wall.

Next I'm adding back details: a battery-pack graphic with bolts and lettering for the torso's rear panel, plus red shoulder straps that arc over the top from front to back near the neck gap to suggest the kid is wearing the box like a backpack.

Still defining strap geometry...

Actually, I'm reconsidering the straps—they'd overlap the front panel awkwardly at those x-coordinates, so I think it's simpler to drop them entirely rather than force visible stubs, and focus instead on adding folded flaps along the torso's top edge.

For the flap detail, I'm weighing whether to show a corrugated cardboard rim at the top edges, but since the helmet mostly covers that gap, I'll instead let the small visible opening reveal the kid's neck and shoulders beneath, showing a glimpse of their blue-yellow shirt.

Adding sloped shoulder geometry, a neck sweep connecting torso to head, and considering a pelvis sphere to suggest the jeans hip area where the box bottom leaves a gap.

I'm also thinking about reinforcing the torso box corners with thin duct-tape strip geometry along the vertical edges to add visual detail.

I'll finish with loops. For tape, I'll use a silvery duct-tape texture with fine streaks and a tan packing-tape color across the helmet and torso seams. I also want to decorate the torso side panels with a sketched lightning bolt and star details around the arm holes for a fun touch.

Working out the orientation math for the side planes so the textures face correctly...

I work out the viewBox mapping so the hole lands at v=35, placing the gear ring decal there at (75,35) with radius 36, alongside the lightning bolt, stars, and "PUSH" arrow decals, plus simpler cardboard seam lines. Then I move on to the helmet, centering it at (0,1.16,0) with 0.37 dimensions.

Now I'm designing the helmet box as a hollow cardboard shell: front, back, left, right, and top panels around a window cutout, each 8mm thick, with the window framed by top/bottom/side bars so the kid's head is visible inside against the kraft-colored interior.

Actually a single textured front plane would block the window underneath, unless I use alpha cutout so the window area stays transparent while marker doodles render elsewhere. That's cleaner than separate bars—one decal plane over the front with transparency everywhere except the drawn details, leaving the window region see-through.

I'm mapping out the SVG coordinates for the window cutout and planning the doodles: lightning-bolt eyebrows and antenna wires near the top, a speaker-grille pattern on the bottom bar, gears on the left side, a star on the right, plus a red tape border drawn as a stroked rectangle around the window frame.

For the helmet sides I'm placing concentric-circle speaker grilles at ear height, with small 3D ear tube stubs built from cylinder geometry capped with foil-colored concentric textures, colored like a kraft toilet-paper roll, plus handwritten "L"/"R" labels and star doodles nearby. Now I'm starting on the helmet top plane with vent slats and hat details.

Giving them emissive glow so they read as little lights. For the back of the helmet, I'll add a doodled "ROBO" decal with bolts and a hatch pattern, skipping hair since it's covered. Now I'm shaping the head itself as a scaled sphere, positioning it just above the body.

Working through skin tone with flat cheek coloring, placing squashed ear spheres that stay hidden under the helmet walls, then building a hair cap sphere positioned to cover the top and back while leaving the forehead and fringe visible in front.

I realize a full sphere cap would extend too far forward and cover the face at eye level, so I need to restrict it to a partial sphere using phi/theta angles so the hairline sits above the brows rather than down at eye level.

For the visible cap surface, I'll scatter hair tuft cards filtered to the front-upper region to form the fringe, angling them to flow over the forehead, plus a few standing cowlick cards at the crown, using a brown hair texture with tinted highlights.

Now I'm placing facial decals on the head sphere: eye textures with white sclera, brown iris, black pupil, highlight and lash line, mirrored for both sides, positioned near the upper face and oriented using the skull surface's normal direction so they curve naturally with the head's shape.

I'm checking that the azimuth and elevation math lines up eyes correctly relative to the head center, then moving to brows, a small pink nose bump, and cheek blush decals to round out the face.

Now I'm working out the mouth decal position and jaw hinge geometry, placing the lower jaw sphere relative to the head sphere's bottom edge so the chin sits naturally.

I'll just target the decal to both surfaces without bone-splitting worries, since the jaw stays rigid under the head either way. For the jaw piece itself, I'm sizing a small scaled sphere near the chin position, overlapping with the lower portion of the head sphere to form the lower face.

Decal mostly lands on skull, grin spanning that upper mouth region. For the decal function I'm setting parameters like position, direction, size and optional mirroring/color, letting texture transparency cut away unneeded areas for eyes and other features. Hands keep the same skin tone, and for the shirt I'm figuring out where skin versus fabric shows between the arm segments at elbow and wrist gaps.

Mapping the arm into segments: skin-colored sweep overall, yellow sleeve from shoulder to elbow gap, a foil tube for the upper arm, bare skin at the elbow joint, a red-painted forearm tube, then skin again at the wrist with a small rubber cuff band. I'm defining rod geometry for the tubes with radius and segment counts bound to the shoulder and elbow joints, plus adding colored tape rings at the tube ends for a corrugated foil look.

I'm now reconsidering the forearm material — maybe a cardboard tube painted red with a white stripe, or banded paint sections in kraft and red tones, versus a blue acrylic-painted tube with silver duct tape bands at the joints. I'm also thinking about adding a red sweatband at the wrist and possibly a name-tag sticker reading something like "HELLO I AM ROBO-MAX" on the lower torso panel.

Tallying up the part count across pelvis, legs, shins, shoes, torso, helmet, face, hair, arms, and antennas, I'm landing around 250 total, which fits within my target range, so no merging needed. Now I'm defining the kraft color palette constants before writing the full construction code.

Writing paint functions...

Finishing the color blending with a highlight tint, then checking the sine period makes sense for the scale and confirming top faces use the right coordinate. I'm now planning the paint coverage on the texture sheet, noting that all the box wall surfaces need painting.

Writing foil material shader... then checking that cell-noise helpers are properly exported from the paint module before moving on to defining the duct tape texture with a grainy silver tone.

For denim I'll just use grain, and skin stays flat. Now I'm writing a helper function that makes meshes glow by cloning their materials and setting emissive color and intensity based on the original color and texture map.

For textured screen planes, I want the material color to be white with the texture map applied as emissive so it reads as self-lit. I'm also planning a slab box helper that creates box geometry parts with position, color, and bone attachment, making sure to explicitly assign bones like chest for torso or head for helmet rather than relying on nearest-joint inference.

Now I'm checking the spine joint spans to confirm the chest bone lines up correctly with the torso box, then moving on to writing the SVG texture for the torso front panel.

Writing SVG code...

Rather than hand-coding each gauge tick, I'm planning to generate them programmatically with a loop that computes angle positions around the semicircle, keeping the needle and red zone arc consistent.

Now I'm working out the panel sliders and screen frame placement, deciding to draw the screen as its own slightly offset element in front so it reads as a glowing 3D plane rather than flat on the panel.

Next I'm laying out the row of number buttons as outlined circles with 3D caps on top and small labels underneath, then starting on the vent grille with horizontal slats in the lower-left section.

Adding X-marked corner bolts, slightly wobbly hand-drawn strokes, and comic-style labels. For TORSO_BACK I'm sketching a big green battery with a "+" terminal, "MAX ROBOT" lettering, tape cross, and a power cord, keeping it to about 15 elements; for TORSO_SIDE I'm building a toothed gear ring around the center hole using a polygon-generating function.

Still writing gear geometry...

I'm adding the classic cardboard "THIS SIDE UP" arrow label and fragile glass icon on the bottom of the side panel, keeping orientation readable from outside on both left and right planes. For the helmet side view, I'm positioning the ear at center with concentric dashed rings forming a speaker doodle.

Now I'm working out the orientation math for the top plane, figuring out local axes and the up vector so the drawing faces correctly toward the back when the helmet is viewed from above.

Okay, that orientation checks out with north mapping to -Z and east to +X, so the viewer-from-above arrangement is consistent. For the top drawing I'll keep it simple: vents, a piece of tape, and a star sticker placed near the top panel surface, and I need to nail down the exact y-coordinates for the panel's thickness and center.

Now I'm defining the helmet's wall boxes -- top, back, left, right, and the front bars for vents -- with their positions and dimensions, and I'm checking for overlapping coplanar faces between the top wall and side walls that could cause z-fighting at the shared edges.

Refining bar and wall dimensions to avoid overlap...

I'll skip the SVG rim and just use 3D tape boxes instead. Checking visibility — the face sits behind the window glass so the camera should see it fine through the opening, and the helmet interior depth clears the head geometry properly. I'm also placing ear tubes as small cylinders extending outward on either side of the helmet.

Adding ear tube end caps...

Now I'm positioning antenna stubs on top of the helmet, small kraft-colored cylinders anchored near the crown, then building spring-coil antennas above them using a helix of small radius turns following a tilted outward direction.

For the tips, I'm giving the left one a glowing red sphere and the right one a flat five-point foil star extruded slightly in thickness so it faces forward, both mounted on the bone head of the antenna spring.

Now moving to the torso, I'm planning extra 3D detailing: small colored slide-handle boxes at the three slider positions, plus four round bottle caps in red, yellow, green, and blue arranged in a row near the gauge panel.

I'm skipping the emergency button and vent slats, but adding a couple of small glowing LED spheres tucked into the panel corners near the vents for a bit of extra detail.

For the screen I'm adding a dark recessed box with the ink detail offset slightly, then layering a glowing plane above it with the heart/ECG graphic. I'm debating whether to add a coiled cable element but deciding to skip it since it would cross other details—opting to leave the torso clean instead.

I'm also adding box details like duct-taped corners and a packing-tape seam, plus a shipping label with a barcode and "FRAGILE" text on the torso back. For the shin boxes I'm designing a red-bordered "FRAGILE" sticker with a wine glass icon to place on the front face of each shin box, working out the exact positioning so it fits within the box dimensions without clipping into the shoe.

Checking the leg geometry now — ankle and hip x-offsets, box widths, and gaps between the two shin boxes to make sure they don't overlap and the shoes/heels still clear properly. I'm noticing the torso's hip corners extend further out in x than the thighs sit, so I need to check whether the thighs end up hidden beneath the torso box.

I'm deciding to skip the belt detail to keep things simple, and sketching out the arm chain points (shoulder, elbow, wrist) as a straight sweep for now rather than adding a bend.

Sizing the tube radii for the skin sweep and matching them against the hole ring tolerances so the arm tube fits cleanly through its joint without clipping.

Now I'm working out the hand geometry: palm box positioned past the wrist tip, knuckle position, and finger chain setup parented to the arm's tip joint.

I'm defining finger segment lengths and fanning offsets per finger (index, middle, ring, pinky), with unique joint names per segment and a "digit" role, then sweeping each chain with a hexagonal cross-section skin color.

Checking palm and finger radii match up, and considering whether to add tiny fingernail details on the tips using flattened spheres positioned at the chain's end point.

Now I'm working out the thumb's base and joint positions with two spans, then sizing the palm box to make sure it covers the base of the fingers and thumb edge properly.

For the arm I'm reusing the same build mirrored with a side sign, deriving L/R from whether x is positive or negative. Then I'm setting up hips as the root parent for the leg chain, and starting to define the jaw joint hinge relative to the head, aiming it forward.

Now I'm defining the head and neck joints as a chain under the chest, with the neck's skin built as a rigid sweep bound to the neck bone.

For the head, I'm attaching a scaled sphere skull geometry to the head bone, keeping it low-poly but smooth-shaded. I'm starting to lay out face elements, picking a skin tone color and a blush accent to add later.

Now I'm sketching the eye SVG: an almond-shaped white base with a brown outline, layered iris circles shading from brown to near-black toward the pupil, and small white highlight dots for shine, plus a lash path along the top.

For the brow, I'm drawing a thick curved stroke in brown, and for the nose I'm keeping it simple as a small sphere. The mouth gets an open-smile path with a dark fill, a white band suggesting upper teeth, a pink tongue ellipse, and an outline stroke -- positioned using angle-based coordinates relative to the head center so it sits correctly on the open jaw.

Checking the geometry, the mouth decal lands right above the jaw sphere's top where they overlap slightly, which works fine since the raycast picks the outermost hit between skull and jaw. I'm adding small ear spheres tucked near the sides of the head, mostly hidden by the helmet anyway, then building a hair cap using a partial sphere with a limited theta range to form a cropped dome, calculating where its rim meets the scalp.

I'm adjusting the rim angle so the hairline sits just outside the skull surface by a few millimeters, then repositioning the brow decals slightly lower so they clear the hairline since fringe cards will droop over the forehead anyway.

Now I'm placing a nape sphere for back hair, scaled and positioned to stay within the overall silhouette bounds, and setting up a scatter pattern for fringe cards across the hair cap surface — filtering by position so they only land on the forward upper region, with tufted hair texture, lean angle, and forward flow direction.

I'm also adding crown tufts with their own scatter filter and flow direction, confirming the scatter function works with area-weighted triangle sampling and enough attempts to satisfy the filtered count, then moving on to defining the hair texture as an SVG.

Now I'm sketching a hair blade shape with a lighter streak and dark outline, finishing the hat and hair layers. I'm also fixing the neck gap by adding a small scaled sphere at the shoulder to simulate a collar, then checking that eyes remain visible under helmet lighting before adding cheek blush decals with small freckle details.

Writing decal placement function...

Thinking about fun extra details now—maybe googly eyes somewhere playful, like stuck on the antenna bulb or the torso box, keeping in mind nothing should block the face.

I keep rejecting most of these novelty ideas like googly eyes, hanging tags, and pipe cleaners as unnecessary clutter, deciding to skip them in favor of simpler details like the existing tape rings on the arm tubes.

Now I'm settling on adding small foil "bolt" accents at the torso panel corners and helmet front using a reusable bolt helper function, while skipping extras like pockets or paper clips. With the decorative details mostly finalized, I'm shifting focus to actually writing the code carefully, keeping TypeScript types correct and avoiding strict-mode issues like unused parameters.

Writing builder helpers for boxes, cylinders, rods, and sweeps...

Writing SVG gauge code...

Writing torso SVG markup...

Still writing panel layout...

I'm extending the ECG line through the heart and adding a rotated name tag sticker with "HELLO my name is MAX" in handwritten style. I'm also adding torn tape pieces at the panel corners using small angled polygons for a sticker-collage effect.

Next I'm adding cross-bolt details to the panel corner screws, then designing the screen SVG with a dark green background, a bright wave line, and a pixel smiley face saying "HI!" with glowing lime eyes and scanline texture. For the back panel I'm drawing a green battery icon with terminals, a lightning bolt, and charge bars.

For the shipping label I'm placing a tilted white rectangle with vertical barcode lines, "TO: MOM & DAD" text, a red "FRAGILE/HANDLE WITH CARE" stamp, and a handwritten "MAX'S ROBOT" marker label. For the torso side panel I'm laying out a gear shape, bolt, up-arrows with "THIS SIDE UP" text, plus a lightning bolt and stars, and I'm writing a helper function to generate the gear tooth path geometry.

For the helmet front plate I'm sketching the layout: leaving the transparent window area empty, drawing yellow lightning bolt doodles flanking the top bar on both sides, and placing three bottle-cap-style light details centered along the top bar.

Now I'm adding side-bar doodles—a gear and bolts on the left, a star, heart, and arrows on the right—plus vertical grille slats across the bottom bar to mimic a speaker mouth. I'm working through the exact pixel-to-millimeter mapping for the window and bar widths so everything lines up proportionally.

For the helmet side texture, I'm placing the ear tube centered with a dashed ring, small sound-wave arcs, corner bolts, directional arrows, and scribbled "BEEP"/"BOOP" text for playful detail. I'm then moving on to lay out the top-view texture with multiple vent openings.

For the back panel, I'm adding bold "ROBO" lettering with cross-tape and computing the correct UV axis mapping so the wall's texture orientation matches the viewer's perspective from behind, with right mapping to -X. Then I'm starting to work out how the circular ear geometry crops into its drawn viewBox.

I'm sketching the ear as concentric speaker-foil rings with a red accent ring and silver gradient shading, then moving to the FRAGILE shin sticker — a red-bordered rectangle with glass icon positioned on the shin's front face — before considering (and mostly skipping) smaller details like shoe laces and star decals.

Still placing the star patch...

Counting up textures now - I'm at 16 total (torso faces, screen, helmet parts, facial features, hair, fragile mark, star patch), which is above my 5-12 target but shouldn't hurt as long as the atlas stays under 4096px, so I'm thinking about trimming some down.

Keeping sizes moderate for most textures, mirroring brow geometry rather than giving it its own texture, and keeping the small star patch at 128px. Now I'm starting to write the actual build code, setting up the project metadata and paint size before defining the skeleton joints starting with the hips as the root.

I realize I need to avoid a zero-length bone between hips and the first spine joint, so I'm offsetting the spine chain's starting position slightly above the hips to create a short but real bone segment.

Now I'm laying out the spine joint positions for spine1, spine2, and chest, then assigning the torso parts like the chest box and pelvis to their corresponding bones. Next I'm setting up the legs as a chain parented to the hips.

I'll taper the leg sweep radii smoothly with three keys, paint denim-colored grain for jeans, and consider adding a knee patch via decal cards, though I might skip that detail for now.

Adding a yellow patch with slight embedding, then defining a toe joint parented to the leg tip with a "digit" role, positioned and aimed outward for the foot structure, and computing the shoe part offsets from the leg side.

Now I'm placing shoe geometry: a heel sphere sized to meet the sole top, a tilted tongue box for the lace area, a red toe upper sphere, a white toe cap, and a series of thin white lace boxes across the top of the shoe.

Then I'm defining the sole as two white boxes (heel and toe) sized and positioned so they meet with a slight overlap, and adding a small white cylinder for the sock ring at the ankle opening.

For the torso, I'm setting up box dimensions and position attached to the chest joint, treating it as a solid board shape that other parts like tape and dials will attach to, and considering whether to add cut-out edges at the bottom opening near the pelvis.

Then I'm adding decal planes for the front, back, and side torso textures positioned relative to the chest, plus a hole cylinder for ventilation with a brown ink color and a torus-shaped tape ring wrapping around it.

Writing cap geometry logic...

Positioning duct tape pieces...

Skip torso top for now, add neck gap. For the helmet I want brown packing tape strips at the top-front edge and along the top rim, drawn in the top SVG view, plus smaller torn-end tape pieces on the sides. I'm also keeping an eye on total line count to stay organized, and sketching out a brad helper function for placing bolt spheres on the helmet.

Now I'm defining a helix function that generates a coiled curve along a direction vector using perpendicular basis vectors, useful for things like coiled cables or springs, making sure the lead end starts properly attached to its base stub.

I'm also working out a star-outline generator that alternates between outer and inner radii at each vertex, with an optional "sharp" marker type for corner points used during extrusion.

For the extrude call itself, I'm setting up the orientation axes, thickness, bevel, foil color, and bone attachment for the antenna star, confirming the paint color maps correctly onto extruded geometry. I also need to verify a knee patch using a raycast against the leg sweep surface, checking that the ray origin's x-coordinate scales properly with the side parameter so the hit lands correctly on the knee.

Now I'm working through the hair card placement, making sure the hit array only pulls from the leg surface and not other body parts, and guarding against an empty hits array before passing it to the card generator.
